I'm a pragmatist and a rationalist. When people claim something is for specific purposes and serves specific functions such as "Pokemon GO! brings people together and encourages exploration", I evaluate whether the statement is true, and that involves thinking about how it goes about achieving objectives. In this case Pokemon GO! is AR and uses GPS to get people to go places, where they may end up interacting. By encouraging people to go to certain places this does in fact bring them together in a literal sense, but it doesn't allow for the sort of authentic interaction that they'd otherwise have if they met somewhere of their own volition for a more general interest. For example people who go to conventions will often share interest in whatever the convention focuses on, therefore their rapport is more natural and more varied than just "WHOA THERE'S A BULBASAUR IN THIS COFFEE SHOP EVERYBODY", which is more artificial interaction. Because it revolves entirely around a single subject, which once exhausted isn't likely to leave lasting impressions or actual socialization. You celebrate the pokemon and then go away to find more, or just go about your day. So it doesn't really bring people together in a true and decent social sense, if it did you'd probably be hanging out with people from the same team as you, who you met by being part of the same team. But that doesn't really happen, most of your encounters are incidental and tertiary to your focus on Pokemon. As for exploration as others have pointed out the better Pokemon are more concentrated in urban centers and soon places that pay for higher density. I live in a rural area, most Pokemon out here are shitty, just Pidgeys, Rattatas and Zubats. So the further out you go to places that would actually be worth exploring, the less incentive there is to do so. And moreover even if there were you wouldn't be enjoying the exploration, you'd be enjoying the payoff of decent Pokemon. A friend of mine was telling me just yesterday that he went for a jog at a really big, nice forest and was admiring the scenery, then two random Pokemon GO! players came by asking if he'd seen any Pokemon. They weren't looking around for the sake of looking around or admiring the beauty of the environment. They were looking around for Pokemon, and when they found them they'd go elsewhere to find more. Claims that it encourages exploration aren't really true, because they're not really exploring. They're being directed by a GPS to animated fictional creatures, and when they find them they go off to find more, rather than actually interact with their environment authentically and organically. I'll finish off by saying that I'm not attacking the game, I'm criticizing it. People claim it does certain things to/for the people who're playing it, and in a technical, practical and realistic sense it isn't. Hopefully from this you'll see that I'm not "hating everything", and I'm not irrational about what I AM doing, which is forming an educated view on a subject. Advice to you would be to grow up and perhaps acknowledge that there are alternative viewpoints, and if you take a break from being a self-absorbed, heavily biased asshole you might find yourself growing as a person.

You are witnessing the mainstream birth of a new genre: "augmented reality" gaming, designed to get people out of their homes and out into stores, eateries, and businesses.

The game/server-side is paid for by user microtransactions and for merchants/entities that pay to register their business location as a "stop". Eventually, there will be ads on "stops" and movie trailers and such.

The businesses have an interest in this because it gets more foot traffic to their doorsteps. Some businesses even buy Lures to get people to come in and eat/drink while catching Pokemon.

Users get a sort of in-person social interaction that measures around being a lighter level of more involved games like D&D or Magic The Gathering, with a broader level of access.

Now instead of your phone being an "App" gateway to see what's downtown, people will be constantly logged into their game, collecting items or battling creatures, and being exposed to businesses and eateries they may never usually visit or tread near.

The marketing goldmine of data on the whereabout of players, travel patterns, how long they spend at each spot, is probably worth billions.

I suspect there will be other games in this genre to come. Like a "Dragon Quest GO" where you roll your own hero, choose a class, and then get into random battles, earning XP, leveling up, finding treasure chests/items at "stops", grouping with your friends, and taking on enemy towers. etc.

The only losers to this new genre are Xbox Live, PSN, and MMORPGS: The players that were previously casual gamers on Xbox Live, PSN, and MMORPGs on PCs. These players have disappeared from those networks and have gone outside, thinning the online gaming population to just the "hardcore" people, which will get to be sucky without no easy prey to kill/defeat.

The casuals may even go so far as to end their monthly subscriptions for those services because they're having too much fun outside, potentially with fellow augmented reality gamers they've met in real life because of the game.
